## Coordinating action
Request, propose and negotiate shared or individual action.
Boundary: Require a successful request, proposal, commitment or response about action. Merely describing a desire or future event is insufficient.

Assess requests, offers or invitations, suggestions, commitments, acceptance or refusal, and negotiation of plans. A request tries to get an addressee to act; an offer makes the speaker’s help available. A suggestion proposes a shared option without necessarily settling it. A future statement becomes a commitment only when the exchange supports an undertaking. A short acceptance can succeed after an identifiable invitation. A copied polite formula without a recoverable action is absent. Distinguish permission questions from action requests using context, rather than crediting every possible action function. Evaluate addressee agreement and politeness in the selected variety. Do not require a particular courtesy phrase or formal imperative when an ordinary conversational request is already successful.

Evaluate imperative and interrogative request constructions with their actual addressee. Formal agreement and linking vowels are relevant to the form used, but one isolated error need not erase a clearly successful action function.

## Feelings and viewpoints
Express internal states, evaluations and positions.
Boundary: Require a correctly expressed feeling, desire, preference or position. An ordinary factual assertion is not automatically an opinion.

Assess desire, preference, emotion, opinion and agreement or disagreement. A desire construction names a wanted state or action; a future statement alone need not do so. A comparison of liking expresses preference. An emotional adjective can report a feeling without an overt present copula. An opinion marker can frame a judgment, while an agreement or rejection expression explicitly takes a stance on an identifiable proposition. A short choice can answer a preference question contextually; a drink name in an inventory does not establish liking. A bare acknowledgement need not mean agreement. A copied feeling word with no recoverable experiencer or stance is absent. Judge agreement and negation against the selected variety, preserving ordinary subject omission and avoiding an English-only model of how feelings must be expressed.

Recognize أُرِيدُ with أَنْ, agreement verbs and nominal feeling predicates. Do not confuse a polite request with a report of personal preference merely because it contains a desire verb.

## Information exchange
Seek, supply and verify information relevant to the exchange.
Boundary: Require successful information seeking or a relevant informative response. Question-shaped requests for action do not qualify just for their form.

Look for an actual information question, relevant answer, factual check or useful detail. Questions can use an interrogative expression or suitable interrogative delivery; English-style auxiliary inversion is not required. A clock time can answer a recoverable closing-time question without repeating the event. Confirmation supplies a candidate proposition and asks whether it holds. Detail must help resolve the current information need, not merely lengthen a message. A copied question word without an identifiable request is absent. A capability-shaped question asking the listener to do something usually coordinates action rather than merely asking about capacity. A request to repeat an unheard message repairs conversation. Judge question forms and short answers in the selected variety, including colloquial particles and omitted material recoverable from the exchange.

Recognize formal interrogatives and confirmation expressions. Case and word order must be evaluated within the chosen question construction, without imposing English question syntax.

## Managing conversation
Establish contact, coordinate turns and repair mutual understanding.
Boundary: Require a successful opening, response, turn/topic action or repair. Sending any message or quoting a greeting does not automatically qualify.

Assess opening or closing an exchange, acknowledging, asking for clarification, rephrasing, correcting misunderstanding, and managing turns or topics. A greeting can open contact. An acknowledgement may show receipt without agreement. A clarification question targets unclear wording or reference in the current exchange. Rephrasing makes an existing meaning clearer; correcting misunderstanding replaces an incorrect interpretation. A topic transition manages the conversation rather than merely mentioning a noun. A short conventional formula can work when its interactional purpose is clear. A copied greeting in a vocabulary list is absent. Do not invent a preceding misunderstanding to credit an isolated unrelated sentence. Evaluate conversational formulas and addressee forms within the selected variety without making Modern Standard prose the default measure of natural colloquial interaction.

Recognize formal greetings, clarification and restatement formulas. A successful brief acknowledgement need not be expanded into a formal full sentence.

## People, things, and places
Establish referents and describe properties, locations, quantities and relationships.
Boundary: Require an identifiable referent and a correctly expressed property, spatial relation, quantity or relationship. Naming alone does not demonstrate every function in this group.

Assess identification, descriptions, location or movement, possession or relationships, and quantity or comparison. A present nominal sentence may identify or describe without an overt be verb. A preposition with a suffixed possessor can express having; an attached possessive suffix can identify whose object it is. Comparison needs a recoverable standard or ordered alternatives, not merely a route number. A place phrase answering a where-question can succeed contextually. A copied demonstrative with no identifiable referent or relation is absent. Judge gender, number, definiteness and construction choices against the selected variety. Do not demand English articles or a have verb, and do not require Modern Standard case endings in Levantine conversation. Clear unsuccessful realization is not successful group evidence; ordinary subject omission is not itself failure.

Use Modern Standard demonstratives, agreement and case where the written or spoken register makes them relevant. Distinguish a definite noun plus indefinite predicate from a definite attributive adjective. Pausal pronunciation is not automatically an error.

## Possibilities and constraints
Express capability, permission, requirements and epistemic limits.
Boundary: Distinguish ability, permission, obligation and likelihood. Similar wording can serve a request instead; judge the actual function.

Recognize ability, permission, obligation, possibility and confidence. Capability and permission can share an expression, with the exchange identifying which is intended. A deadline can ground an obligation. A possibility expression weakens commitment to a proposition, while uncertainty wording reports limited confidence. A contextual grant of permission can be short. A copied modal without a recoverable action or proposition is absent. A polite ability-shaped request does not necessarily assert the listener’s skill. Do not turn ambiguity between two successful subtypes within this group into uncertainty about whether any group function occurred. Distinguish prohibition, inability and lack of necessity. Evaluate negation and following verb forms in the selected variety, and do not require a formal modal construction in colloquial speech.

Recognize formal capability, permission and necessity constructions, including the following subordinate verb. Evaluate لَيْسَ inflection in nominal negation without demanding its use in every negative sentence.

## Reasons and connections
Relate propositions through explanation, consequence, condition, contrast and support.
Boundary: Require a correctly expressed relationship between ideas. Sequence alone is not causation, a condition or an argument.

Assess causes, consequences, conditions, contrast and support for a claim. A reason connective links an outcome to its cause or motivation. A result expression presents the following event as a consequence. A conditional establishes a dependency rather than asserting that its antecedent happened. Contrast requires opposed expectations or alternatives, not just two adjacent clauses. Supporting a claim requires relevant evidence and a recoverable claim; naming a connective alone is absent. A because-fragment can succeed after a clear why-question. Do not impose English conditional tense matching on Arabic constructions. Recognize selected-variety connectives and evaluate the relationship actually expressed, allowing natural omitted material without inventing the missing relationship.

Evaluate formal causal and conditional syntax, including clause linking appropriate to the consequence. A perfect-form verb after إِذَا can refer to a future condition.

## Time and events
Locate events in time and express their temporal structure.
Boundary: One correctly expressed temporal relationship is sufficient. Present properties alone do not establish temporal skill. Judge meaning in context, not a tense label.

Assess current, past and future events, duration or recurrence, sequence and event phase. Past conjugation can locate an event before the speech time; future particles combine with a suitable verb form. Time adverbs and the exchange can establish reference without a unique mandatory tense marker. Frequency requires a recurring interval or equivalent context. Finishing an activity is event-phase evidence, whereas a past event alone need not entail completion. An answer meaning yesterday can succeed after a clear when-question. A copied time word with no recoverable event is absent. Do not demand English progressive auxiliaries or overt subject pronouns. Evaluate verbal prefixes, aspect and negation within the selected variety; do not mistake a legitimate colloquial form for broken Modern Standard Arabic.

Evaluate past and imperfect morphology, contextual time and future سَـ or سَوْفَ. Do not demand an explicit pronoun when conjugation supplies the subject. Formal agreement depends on the actual construction.
